title: Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex: Sharper, sportier streetfighter
content: When Royal Enfield introduced the Guerrilla 450 back in 2024, it was envisioned as a stripped-back, urban-focused sibling to the adventure-touring Himalayan 450. Sharing the high-performance Sherpa engine, the roadster stood out for its punchy character and aggressive road manners. Two years on, the Chennai-based bike manufacturer is back with a performance-focused iteration designed to up the ante: the Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex. Here is a closer look at what makes this variant special. Striking the right stance: Design and ergonomics While the underlying silhouette of the Guerrilla remains intact, the Apex introduces key changes to deliver a significantly sportier riding experience. The most noticeable revision is the riding geometry. The bike features a newly designed, wider aluminium handlebar that has been repositioned 56 mm lower and pulled 57 mm forward compared to the standard variant. This shift moves the rider's centre of gravity forward, putting more weight over the front wheel for an aggressive, attack-ready posture that dramatically changes how the motorcycle responds to inputs. Visual updates are subtle yet effective. A small, sleek headlamp cowl and a removable rear seat cowl lend the Apex a much sharper, single-seater aesthetic when riding solo. It also gets eye-catching graphics package available in three new striking colourways: Apex Red, Apex Green, and Apex Black. Notably, the 43 mm front telescopic forks now ditch the fork gaiters of the standard model for a cleaner look. Crucially, the dual-purpose Ceat tyres have been swapped out for premium 17-inch Vredestein Centuro ST Plus radials, geared specifically for superior grip and confidence while leaning into fast corners. Smart features and tech In terms of instrumentation, the Apex retains the high-resolution 4-inch circular TFT digital console. Boasting full-screen map navigation, the display can be paired with a smartphone to handle music playback, phone calls, and incoming notifications. Navigating the menus remains intuitive, managed entirely through the tactile handlebar-mounted joystick. The heart of the beast: Engine and performance At its core lies the same 452 cc liquid-cooled, single-cylinder DOHC 4-valve engine. This Sherpa unit pumps out 40.02 PS at 8000 RPM and a peak torque of 40 Nm at 5500 RPM, paired with a smooth-shifting 6-speed gearbox and an assist-and-slip clutch. However, Royal Enfield has recalibrated the ride-by-wire system. The throttle response has been significantly optimised, offering crisper feedback in both Street and Sport modes. The power delivery is linear, but it is the urgent low-end torque that truly brings the ride to life. The engine absolutely shines in the mid-range and top-end, making highway overtakes effortless. A welcome refinement is the improved response in first and second gears, largely eliminating low-speed jerky on-off throttle transitions. Combined with the aggressive riding posture and wider handlebar, chucking the 185 kg motorcycle into quick transitions is delightfully easy. Crucially, the low 780 mm seat height makes it remarkably accessible for riders of all statures. Handling and ride quality With telescopic forks up front and a pre-load adjustable monoshock at the rear, the suspension setup tilts slightly toward the firmer side. This stiffness pays massive dividends when negotiating smooth tarmac and fast, sweeping corners, keeping the chassis exceptionally stable and composed. On the flip side, sharp bumps and broken inner-city roads do filter through to the rider, sacrificing some outright plushness. Anchorage is handled by ventilated disc brakes on both ends—a 310 mm rotor at the front and a 270 mm unit at the back—backed up by a well-calibrated dual-channel ABS. Verdict and pricing The Royal Enfield Guerrilla 450 Apex is tailored for riders seeking pure riding thrills on weekend sprints and twisty mountain roads...
